summary: This is the rule catalog behind Emil Kowalski's review-animations skill: the exact values, curves and rules a motion review should cite instead of approximating. It covers whether to animate by frequency of use, easing by motion type with three strong custom cubic-bezier curves, a per-element duration table with a sub-300ms UI rule, physical correctness (no scale(0), trigger-origin popovers, press feedback), spring configs, interruptibility, asymmetric timing, GPU-only performance, transforms and clip-path techniques, drag gestures, crossfade blur, stagger, accessibility, debugging and cohesion. For a design system it is close to a ready-made motion token set and rulebook: the curves, durations, spring parameters and thresholds can become locked tokens and lint checks.
key_ideas: Frequency decides whether to animate: 100+/day and keyboard actions never animate, rare moments can delight.
Easing is chosen by motion type, with ease-out as the default and ease-in banned on UI.
Built-in CSS easings are too weak; three strong custom curves cover UI, on-screen movement and drawers.
Each element type has a duration band, and UI animation stays under 300ms.
Nothing appears from nothing: start from scale(0.9–0.97) with opacity, scale popovers from the trigger, keep modals centered.
Springs have no fixed duration and keep velocity when interrupted; the Apple-style duration-plus-bounce config is recommended.
Transitions retarget mid-animation while keyframes restart, so rapid UI uses transitions or @starting-style.
Slow where the user decides, fast where the system responds.
Only transform and opacity are animated; a CSS variable on a parent recalcs every child's styles, and Framer Motion shorthands drop frames under load.
clip-path: inset() and percentage translates are versatile tools for reveals, overlays, tabs and drawers.
Drag dismissal uses velocity, boundary damping, pointer capture, multi-touch protection and friction instead of hard stops.
A small blur masks imperfect crossfades; stagger groups by 30–80ms without blocking interaction.
Reduced motion keeps opacity and color but drops movement; hover motion is gated to fine pointers.
Feel is checked in slow motion, frame-by-frame, on real devices and with fresh eyes.
Motion should match the component's personality, as Sonner's slightly slower ease shows.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: A frequency table decides whether to animate; valid purposes are spatial consistency, state indication, explanation, feedback and preventing jarring change.

topics.name: Easing and timing
topics.summary: Easing by motion type (ease-out default, never ease-in on UI), three custom cubic-bezier curves, per-element durations, the sub-300ms UI rule and asymmetric timing.

topics.name: Spring animation
topics.summary: Apple-style { duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 } recommended, a traditional mass/stiffness/damping alternative, subtle bounce 0.1–0.3, and useSpring for decorative mouse tracking.

topics.name: Animation performance
topics.summary: Only transform and opacity, no parent CSS variables driving child transforms, full transform strings instead of Framer Motion shorthands, CSS over JS under load, and WAAPI.

topics.name: Gestures and drag
topics.summary: Velocity-based momentum dismissal, damping at boundaries, pointer capture, multi-touch protection, and friction over hard stops.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Button press feedback at scale(0.97) with a 160ms ease-out transition, and asymmetric press/release timing for a press-and-hold clip-path overlay.

topics.name: Reduced motion

topics.name: Modals and popovers

topics.name: Design taste and judgement

topics.name: Design process

rules.rule: Cite the exact values in this reference in review findings instead of approximating.
rules.why: These are the precise values behind the review.
rules.evidence: Cite these in findings instead of approximating

rules.rule: Do not animate actions used 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts and the command palette toggle.
rules.why: No animation. Ever.

rules.rule: Remove or drastically reduce animation on actions used tens of times a day, such as hover effects and list navigation.
rules.why: Frequency table decision for tens of times/day.

rules.rule: Give occasional UI such as modals, drawers and toasts standard animation.
rules.why: Frequency table decision for occasional use.

rules.rule: Add delight only to rare or first-time moments such as onboarding, feedback and celebrations.
rules.why: Frequency table decision for rare/first-time use.

rules.rule: Never animate keyboard-initiated actions.
rules.why: They repeat hundreds of times daily; animation makes them feel slow and disconnected.

rules.rule: Animate only for a valid purpose: spatial consistency, state indication, explanation, feedback, or preventing a jarring change.
rules.why: These are the valid purposes for motion.

rules.rule: Do not justify motion on a frequently seen element with 'it looks cool'.
rules.why: 'It looks cool' on a frequently-seen element is not valid.

rules.rule: Use ease-out for elements entering or exiting.
rules.why: It starts fast and feels responsive.

rules.rule: Use ease-in-out for elements moving or morphing on screen.
rules.why: Easing decision order for on-screen movement.

rules.rule: Use ease for hover and color changes.
rules.why: Easing decision order for hover and color.

rules.rule: Use linear for constant motion such as marquees and progress.
rules.why: Easing decision order for constant motion.

rules.rule: Default to ease-out when no other easing case applies.
rules.why: Easing decision order default.

rules.rule: Never use ease-in on UI.
rules.why: It starts slow, delaying the exact moment the user is watching; ease-out at 200ms feels faster than ease-in at 200ms.

rules.rule: Use the strong custom curve cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) as the ease-out for UI instead of the built-in ease-out.
rules.why: Built-in CSS easings are too weak.

rules.rule: Use cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) as the ease-in-out for on-screen movement.
rules.why: Built-in CSS easings are too weak.

rules.rule: Use cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) for iOS-like drawers.
rules.why: It is the iOS-like drawer curve (Ionic).

rules.rule: Find easing curves at easing.dev or easings.co instead of hand-rolling them from scratch.
rules.why: Don't hand-roll from scratch.
rules.evidence: Find curves at easing.dev or easings.co

rules.rule: Keep button press feedback at 100–160ms.
rules.why: Duration table value.

rules.rule: Keep tooltips and small popovers at 125–200ms.
rules.why: Duration table value.

rules.rule: Keep dropdowns and selects at 150–250ms.
rules.why: Duration table value; a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.

rules.rule: Keep modals and drawers at 200–500ms.
rules.why: Duration table value.

rules.rule: Allow longer durations only for marketing or explanatory animation.
rules.why: Marketing / explanatory can be longer.

rules.rule: Keep UI animations under 300ms.
rules.why: A 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.

rules.rule: Make loading spinners spin faster.
rules.why: Faster spinners make load feel faster for the same actual time.

rules.rule: After the first tooltip in a toolbar has shown, show later tooltips instantly, skipping both the delay and the animation.
rules.why: Instant tooltips after the first make a toolbar feel faster.

rules.rule: Never animate from scale(0); start from scale(0.9–0.97) with opacity: 0.
rules.why: Nothing in the real world appears from nothing.

rules.rule: Scale popovers from their trigger with transform-origin: var(--transform-origin), not from center.
rules.why: Origin-aware popovers scale from the trigger.

rules.rule: Keep modals at transform-origin: center.
rules.why: Modals appear centered in the viewport, so they are exempt from trigger origin.

rules.rule: Give every pressable element press feedback of transform: scale(0.97) on :active with transition: transform 160ms ease-out.
rules.why: Button press feedback applies to any pressable element.

rules.rule: Keep press-feedback scale subtle, between 0.95 and 0.98.
rules.why: Press feedback should be subtle.

rules.rule: Use springs for drag with momentum, 'alive' elements such as the Dynamic Island, interruptible gestures and decorative mouse tracking.
rules.why: Springs simulate physics, settle on parameters rather than a fixed duration, and feel natural.

rules.rule: Prefer the Apple-style spring config { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }.
rules.why: It is easier to reason about and is recommended.

rules.rule: Use a traditional physics spring { type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 } only when you need more control.
rules.why: Traditional physics gives more control.

rules.rule: Keep spring bounce subtle, between 0.1 and 0.3.
rules.why: Bounce should be subtle.

rules.rule: Avoid bounce in most UI; reserve it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.
rules.why: Bounce belongs to specific interactions, not general UI.

rules.rule: Use springs for gestures users may reverse mid-motion.
rules.why: Springs maintain velocity when interrupted; keyframes restart from zero.

rules.rule: For decorative mouse-following motion, interpolate with useSpring rather than tying the value directly to mouse position.
rules.why: Direct tying feels artificial and has no momentum.

rules.rule: Do not spring-smooth mouse-tied motion unless the motion is decorative.
rules.why: Only do this when the motion is decorative.

rules.rule: Use CSS transitions for anything triggered rapidly, such as toasts being added or toggles.
rules.why: Transitions can be interrupted and retargeted mid-animation, so they are smoother.

rules.rule: Avoid @keyframes animations for dynamic UI.
rules.why: Keyframes restart from zero and cannot be retargeted.
rules.evidence: Not interruptible — avoid for dynamic UI

rules.rule: Use @starting-style for entry animations without JS.
rules.why: It gives entry animation without JS, on top of an interruptible transition.

rules.rule: Where @starting-style is unavailable, fall back to useEffect(() => setMounted(true), []) with a data-mounted attribute.
rules.why: Legacy fallback for entry animation.

rules.rule: Make motion slow where the user is deciding and fast where the system responds.
rules.why: Asymmetric timing matches deliberate action versus system response.

rules.rule: For a press-and-hold overlay (.button:active .overlay), run the press phase slow and linear and the release phase fast with ease-out.
rules.why: Press is deliberate; release is a system response.

rules.rule: Animate only transform and opacity.
rules.why: They skip layout and paint and run on the GPU.

rules.rule: Do not animate padding, margin, height, width, top or left.
rules.why: They trigger all three rendering steps.

rules.rule: Do not drive child transforms through a CSS variable on the parent; set transform directly on the element.
rules.why: A parent variable recalculates styles for all children; a direct transform touches only that element.
rules.evidence: Don't drive child transforms via a CSS variable on the parent

rules.rule: Use the full transform string in Framer Motion (animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}) instead of x/y/scale shorthands.
rules.why: Shorthands are not hardware-accelerated; they run on the main thread via rAF and drop frames under load.
rules.evidence: Framer Motion shorthands are NOT hardware-accelerated

rules.rule: Use CSS for predetermined motion and JS for dynamic or interruptible motion.
rules.why: CSS animations run off the main thread and beat JS under load; rAF-based animations stutter while the browser loads, scripts or paints.
rules.evidence: CSS animations beat JS under load

rules.rule: Use WAAPI (element.animate) when you need JS control with CSS performance.
rules.why: WAAPI is hardware-accelerated, interruptible and needs no library.

rules.rule: Move elements by their own size with translate percentages such as translateY(100%) rather than hardcoded pixels.
rules.why: Percentages are relative to the element's own size regardless of dimensions; Sonner and Vaul position toasts and drawers this way.

rules.rule: Use scale() for press feedback so children (font, icons, content) scale with the element.
rules.why: scale() scaling children is a feature for press feedback.

rules.rule: Use rotateX/Y with transform-style: preserve-3d for depth, orbit or flip effects without JS.
rules.why: 3D transforms give depth, orbit and flip without JS.

rules.rule: Reveal content on scroll by animating clip-path from inset(0 0 100% 0) to inset(0 0 0 0).
rules.why: clip-path: inset(t r b l) eats in from each side and is a powerful animation tool.

rules.rule: Build hold-to-delete overlays with an animated clip-path.
rules.why: Listed use of clip-path: inset().

rules.rule: Make tab color transitions seamless by duplicating the tabs and clipping the active copy.
rules.why: Listed use of clip-path: inset().

rules.rule: Build comparison sliders with clip-path.
rules.why: Listed use of clip-path: inset().

rules.rule: Dismiss swipeable elements by velocity: compute Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs and dismiss if it exceeds about 0.11.
rules.why: A flick should be enough.

rules.rule: Do not require crossing a distance threshold to dismiss a swipe.
rules.why: A flick should be enough.

rules.rule: Damp drags past a natural edge so the element moves less the further you drag.
rules.why: Real things slow before stopping.

rules.rule: Capture the pointer once dragging starts.
rules.why: The drag continues when the pointer leaves the element's bounds.

rules.rule: Ignore extra touch points after a drag begins (if (isDragging) return).
rules.why: Prevents jumps.

rules.rule: Allow over-drag with rising resistance instead of an invisible hard stop.
rules.why: Friction over hard stops.

rules.rule: When a crossfade still shows two overlapping states after tuning easing and duration, add filter: blur(2px) during the transition.
rules.why: It blends them into one perceived transformation.

rules.rule: Keep animated blur under 20px.
rules.why: Heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari.

rules.rule: Stagger group entrances with 30–80ms between items.
rules.why: Stated as the stagger rule; longer delays feel slow.

rules.rule: Do not use stagger delays longer than 30–80ms between items.
rules.why: Longer delays feel slow.

rules.rule: Never block interaction while a stagger plays.
rules.why: Stagger is decorative.

rules.rule: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, keep opacity and color animation and drop transform-based motion.
rules.why: Reduced motion keeps comprehension aids and removes movement.

rules.rule: Gate hover motion behind @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
rules.why: Touch fires false hovers on tap.

rules.rule: In React, read useReducedMotion and remove positional movement when it is on, for example closedX = reduce ? 0 : '-100%'.
rules.why: Reduced motion removes movement and position changes.

rules.rule: Do not remove all animation for reduced motion; keep transitions that aid comprehension and remove movement and position changes.
rules.why: Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations, not zero.
rules.evidence: Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations, not zero

rules.rule: Check motion feel in slow motion by raising duration 2–5× or using the DevTools animation inspector, verifying clean color crossfades, no abrupt easing stop, the right transform-origin, and coordinated properties staying in sync.
rules.why: Recommended in reviews when feel is uncertain.

rules.rule: Step through animations frame by frame in the Chrome DevTools Animations panel to find timing drift between coordinated properties.
rules.why: Frame-by-frame reveals timing drift.

rules.rule: Test gestures such as drawers and swipes on real devices by connecting a phone, hitting the dev server by IP and using Safari remote devtools.
rules.why: Gestures need real devices to judge.

rules.rule: Review motion again with fresh eyes the next day.
rules.why: Imperfections invisible during development surface later.
rules.evidence: imperfections invisible during development surface later

rules.rule: Match motion to the component's personality: playful can be bouncier, a professional dashboard should be crisp and fast.
rules.why: Cohesion between motion and personality makes a component feel right.

rules.rule: For a component meant to feel elegant, consider slightly slower timing and ease rather than ease-out, as Sonner does.
rules.why: Sonner's easing, duration, design and name are in harmony.

rules.rule: Tune opacity plus height for entering and exiting list items by trial and error until it feels right.
rules.why: There is no formula for it.
rules.evidence: Cohesion: Opacity + height in entering/exiting lists

decisions.question: Should this action animate at all, given how often people do it?

options.name: No animation
options.effect: Instant every time; nothing feels slow or disconnected.
options.when: 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts and the command palette toggle.

options.name: Remove or drastically reduce
options.effect: Barely any motion.
options.when: Tens of times a day, such as hover effects and list navigation.

options.name: Standard animation
options.effect: Normal entrance and exit within the duration table.
options.when: Occasional UI such as modals, drawers and toasts.

options.name: Delight
options.effect: Expressive motion.
options.when: Rare or first-time moments such as onboarding, feedback and celebrations.

decisions.recommendation: Use the frequency table; never animate keyboard-initiated actions (Raycast has no open/close animation).

decisions.question: Which easing should this motion use?

options.name: ease-out (cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1))
options.effect: Starts fast and feels responsive.
options.when: Entering or exiting; also the default.

options.name: ease-in-out (cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1))
options.effect: Strong ease-in-out for on-screen movement.

options.name: ease
options.effect: The built-in ease curve.

options.name: linear
options.effect: Even motion for constant movement.

options.name: drawer curve (cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1))
options.effect: iOS-like drawer motion.

decisions.recommendation: Choose by job, default to a strong ease-out, and never use ease-in on UI.

decisions.question: How long should each kind of element animate?

options.name: 100–160ms
options.effect: Snappy press feedback.

options.name: 125–200ms
options.effect: Quick appear and disappear.

options.name: 150–250ms
options.effect: Responsive menus: a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.

options.name: 200–500ms
options.effect: The longest UI band in the table.

options.name: Longer
options.effect: Can run longer than UI motion.

decisions.recommendation: UI animations stay under 300ms; a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.

decisions.question: How should springs be configured?

options.name: Apple-style: duration + bounce
options.effect: { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }; easier to reason about.

options.name: Traditional physics: mass, stiffness, damping
options.effect: { type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }; more control.

decisions.recommendation: Apple-style is recommended; keep bounce at 0.1–0.3 and avoid bounce in most UI.

decisions.question: Should rapidly triggered UI use CSS transitions or keyframes?

options.name: CSS transitions (with @starting-style for entry)
options.effect: Interrupted and retargeted mid-animation.
options.when: Toasts being added, toggles, anything triggered rapidly.

options.name: @keyframes
options.effect: Restart from zero when triggered again.

decisions.recommendation: Transitions for anything triggered rapidly; @starting-style gives entry without JS.

decisions.question: Should this animation run in CSS, WAAPI or JS?

options.name: CSS
options.effect: Runs off the main thread; smooth under load.

options.name: WAAPI
options.effect: JS control with CSS performance, interruptible, no library.
options.when: Programmatic motion that still needs to be smooth.

options.name: JS / springs
options.effect: rAF-based; can stutter while the browser is busy.

decisions.recommendation: CSS for predetermined motion, JS for dynamic and interruptible motion, WAAPI when JS control is needed with CSS performance.

decisions.question: Where should a scaling surface grow from?

options.name: Trigger origin
options.effect: transform-origin: var(--transform-origin); the popover grows out of its trigger.

options.name: Center
options.effect: transform-origin: center; the surface grows in place.
options.when: Modals, which appear centered in the viewport.

decisions.recommendation: Popovers scale from the trigger; modals are exempt and stay centered.

decisions.question: How should a swipe-to-dismiss decide to dismiss?

options.name: Velocity
options.effect: A quick flick dismisses.
options.when: Recommended: dismiss when Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs exceeds about 0.11.

options.name: Distance threshold
options.effect: The user must drag past a set point.

decisions.recommendation: Use velocity; a flick should be enough.

decisions.question: What happens when a drag reaches a boundary?

options.name: Friction
options.effect: Over-drag is allowed with rising resistance.

options.name: Hard stop
options.effect: An invisible wall.

decisions.recommendation: Friction over hard stops, damping more the further past the edge.

decisions.question: When reduced motion is on, should animations become gentler or stop entirely?

options.name: Fewer and gentler
options.effect: Opacity and color remain; movement and position changes go.

options.name: Zero animation
options.effect: Everything stops, including transitions that aid comprehension.
options.when: Rejected: reduced motion does not mean zero.

decisions.recommendation: Fewer and gentler animations, not zero.

decisions.question: Should group items appear one by one?

options.name: Stagger 30–80ms
options.effect: Items cascade in quickly.

options.name: Longer stagger
options.effect: Feels slow.

decisions.recommendation: Stagger by 30–80ms and never block interaction while it plays.

decisions.question: What personality should a component's motion have?

options.name: Bouncier
options.effect: Playful, springy.

options.name: Crisp and fast
options.effect: Professional, efficient.

options.name: Slightly slower with ease
options.effect: Elegant.
options.when: Components meant to feel elegant, as Sonner does.

decisions.recommendation: Match motion to the component's personality so easing, duration, design and name are in harmony.

decisions.question: How should a crossfade that shows two overlapping states be fixed?

options.name: Add a subtle blur
options.effect: filter: blur(2px) blends the states into one perceived transformation.
options.when: After tuning easing and duration has not fixed it.

options.name: Plain crossfade
options.effect: Both states visibly overlap.
options.when: Only if it already looks like one change [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Add blur(2px), keeping blur under 20px because heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari.

process.detail: Place the action in the frequency table (100+/day, tens/day, occasional, rare) and confirm a valid purpose.
Entering or exiting: ease-out; moving or morphing on screen: ease-in-out; hover or color: ease; constant motion: linear; default: ease-out. Use the strong custom curves.
Use the per-element table and keep UI under 300ms.
No scale(0); trigger-origin popovers; centered modals; subtle press feedback.

process.step: Implement interruptibly and on the GPU
process.detail: Transitions or springs for rapid and gesture UI; only transform and opacity; full transform strings; CSS or WAAPI for predetermined motion.
Measure Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs and dismiss when it exceeds about 0.11; capture the pointer; ignore extra touches; damp past edges.
Reduced-motion media query or useReducedMotion that keeps opacity and color and drops movement; gate hover motion to (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
Raise durations 2–5× or use the DevTools animation inspector; check color crossfades, easing endings, transform-origin and property sync.
Use the Chrome DevTools Animations panel to find timing drift between coordinated properties.
For drawers and swipes, connect a phone, open the dev server by IP and use Safari remote devtools.
Review with fresh eyes the next day to catch imperfections invisible during development.

examples.what: Command palette with no open/close animation
examples.visual_note: Cited as correct for something used hundreds of times a day.

examples.what: Easing tokens as CSS custom properties

examples.visual_note: .popover { transform-origin: var(--transform-origin); } so the popover grows from its trigger.
Named as the kind of element springs suit.
.toast { transition: transform 400ms ease; } versus @keyframes slideIn from translateY(100%) to translateY(0).

caveats: This is the reference file of an AI-agent skill, pinned to commit 85e8e23 of emilkowalski/skills (MIT); values can change in later commits.
The sub-300ms UI rule sits beside a 200–500ms band for modals and drawers and 400ms toast examples; the 300ms ceiling does not appear to cover modals, drawers or these toasts [inferred].

The toast examples use plain ease at 400ms, which differs from the ease-out default; the Cohesion section explains Sonner's slightly slower ease as a deliberate choice for elegance, which likely accounts for the toast examples [inferred].
The stagger example uses @keyframes, which the Interruptibility section avoids for rapidly triggered UI; stagger is a one-off group entrance, not a rapid trigger [inferred].
The ~0.11 velocity threshold is written as approximate and has no stated unit; px per ms is implied by distance/elapsedMs [inferred].
The Framer Motion shorthand and rAF performance claims are stated without a benchmark or library version.
var(--transform-origin) is Base UI's variable; other libraries may expose a different name [inferred].
Raycast, Dynamic Island, Sonner and Vaul are single illustrative examples, not surveys.
The Cohesion section tunes opacity plus height for entering and exiting lists, while Performance says not to animate height; list enter/exit appears to be a named exception tuned by feel [inferred].

OpenDesigner's questionnaire suggests different values: Q-motion-06 offers a 20-50ms stagger (this source: 30–80ms) and Q-motion-04's Apple option lists bounce 0 / 0.15 / 0.3 (this source: 0.2 recommended, 0.1–0.3 range). As a non-negotiable source these values should take precedence [inferred].
